::: {.lead}
A mobile game is a program, but it never runs alone. It runs on a processor
that understands only a few hundred simple instructions, under an operating
system that shares the hardware among many programs, inside a platform whose
owner decides how games are built, tested and sold. This chapter defines what
a computing system is, explains how a computer can be understood as a stack of
simpler machines, surveys the families of computers that games run on, and
introduces the idea of a digital platform.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary computing-system hardware software von-neumann cpu memory storage instruction-cycle abstraction-level isa compiler digital-platform >}}

## 1.1 What a computing system is

A **computing system** is a combination of **hardware** (the physical
components), **software** (the programs that control them) and **data**,
organised to perform four functions: it accepts **input** from the outside,
**processes** it by executing instructions, **stores** data for later use, and
produces **output**. The same four functions describe a pocket calculator, a
smartphone and the servers of an online game; what differs is their scale.

### The stored-program computer

Almost every computer in use today follows the design described by John von
Neumann and his colleagues in 1945: the **stored-program** or **von Neumann**
model (@fig-von-neumann). Its key idea is that the *program itself is data*:
the instructions are kept in the same memory as the values they work on, so a
new program can be loaded simply by writing new contents into memory. This is
why one phone can run thousands of different games.

![The stored-program (von Neumann) model. The CPU, the main memory and the input/output devices exchange data over a shared bus.](images/von-neumann.png){#fig-von-neumann width=82%}

The model has four parts:

- the **central processing unit (CPU)**, which contains a *control unit* that
  directs the work, an *arithmetic logic unit (ALU)* that performs arithmetic
  and comparisons, and a few very fast storage cells called *registers*;
- the **main memory (RAM)**, which holds the instructions and data of the
  programs that are running; it is fast but *volatile* — it loses its contents
  when the power is off;
- the **input/output (I/O) devices**, including **storage** (flash memory or
  disks), which keeps programs and files permanently;
- the **bus**, a set of shared connections that carries addresses, data and
  control signals between the parts.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — The instruction cycle"}
The CPU executes a program by repeating the **instruction cycle**:

1. **fetch** the next instruction from main memory;
2. **decode** it — determine which operation it asks for and on which data;
3. **execute** it — perform the operation, for example an addition in the ALU,
   and store the result;

then move on to the next instruction. The rate of this cycle is set by a
clock; a clock rate of 3 GHz means three billion clock ticks per second.
:::

![The instruction cycle, repeated billions of times per second.](images/instruction-cycle.png){#fig-cycle width=62%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — One tap, four functions"}
A player taps the screen to make a character jump.

1. **Input**: the touch screen detects the finger and reports its position
   to the system.
2. **Processing**: the CPU executes the game's instructions: *is the
   character on the ground? then set its upward velocity*; it also checks
   collisions with the platform above.
3. **Output**: the graphics processor draws the new frame; the speaker plays
   the jump sound; the motor may vibrate.
4. **Storage**: when the level ends, the new best score is written to flash
   storage, so that it survives when the phone is switched off.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — How much work fits into one frame?"}
A phone CPU core runs at 3 GHz, and the game targets 60 frames per second.

1. Time per frame: $1/60$ s $\approx 16.7$ ms.
2. Clock ticks per frame: $3 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{1}{60} = 5 \times 10^{7}$,
   that is, 50 million ticks.
3. A modern core completes several instructions per tick, so one frame allows
   roughly a hundred million simple instructions per core. This budget is
   shared by game logic, physics, sound and the operating system.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Confusing **memory** with **storage**. "A phone with 8 GB of memory and
256 GB of storage" has 8 GB of fast, volatile RAM for running programs and
256 GB of slower, permanent flash storage for installed apps and files.
Installing more games fills the storage; running more games at once fills
the memory.
:::

## 1.2 The computer as a multilevel machine

A CPU understands only its own **machine language**: a small set of primitive
instructions such as *load a value from memory*, *add two registers* or *jump
to another instruction if a value is zero*. Writing a game in such
instructions would be impossibly slow. Computer scientists solve this problem
by building a series of **levels of abstraction** on top of the hardware. Each
level defines a language — a set of instructions — that is more convenient
than the one below it, and each level is implemented using the level below.
Tanenbaum calls this view of a computer a **multilevel machine**
(@fig-levels).

![The computer as a multilevel machine, with the levels that a game passes through added at the top.](images/levels.png){#fig-levels width=76%}

| Level | Name | What it provides |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | problem-oriented language | languages such as C#, C++ and Java |
| 4 | assembly language | a readable form of machine instructions |
| 3 | operating system machine | files, processes, memory management, devices |
| 2 | instruction set architecture (ISA) | the machine language of the processor |
| 1 | microarchitecture | the internal data paths, registers and ALU |
| 0 | digital logic | gates built from transistors |

: The six levels of a typical computer (after Tanenbaum). {#tbl-levels}

A program at a higher level is carried down to the hardware in one of two
ways. In **translation**, a program called a **compiler** (or an
*assembler*, for assembly language) converts the whole program into the
language of a lower level before it runs. In **interpretation**, a program
called an **interpreter** reads the higher-level program and carries out each
instruction as it goes. Translation gives faster programs; interpretation is
more flexible. Most modern systems combine the two.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — Instruction set architecture"}
The **instruction set architecture (ISA)** is the level at which hardware and
software meet: the complete list of machine instructions that a family of
processors can execute. Almost all smartphones use the **ARM** ISA; almost
all desktop PCs and current game consoles use **x86-64**. A program compiled
for one ISA does not run directly on another.
:::

The levels explain how one game can reach very different devices. A Unity
game is written in C#. The C# compiler translates it into an intermediate
language (CIL) that belongs to no real processor. For each platform the code
is then translated again into the machine language of that platform's ISA:
ARM for Android and iOS, x86-64 for a Windows PC. The game is written once;
the lower levels are generated for each machine (@fig-builds).

![One C# game, translated for two instruction set architectures.](images/build-targets.png){#fig-builds width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — One line of game code, level by level"}
The line `score = score + 10;` in a C# game is executed as follows.

1. **Level 5**: the programmer writes the line in C#.
2. Translation: the compiler produces CIL, and then ARM instructions for a
   phone — roughly *load* the score from memory into a register, *add* 10,
   *store* the register back to memory.
3. **Level 3**: the operating system has given the game's process the memory
   in which `score` lives, and protects it from other apps.
4. **Levels 2–0**: the processor fetches, decodes and executes the three ARM
   instructions; the ALU's logic gates perform the addition.
:::

## 1.3 Classes of computing systems

Computers range from chips that cost less than a dollar to data centres that
cost billions. In games they appear in five broad classes (@fig-classes),
compared in @tbl-classes.

![Five classes of computing systems used in games.](images/computer-classes.png){#fig-classes width=94%}

| Class | Examples | Typical ISA | Power | Role in games |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| embedded | game controllers, smart toys, VR trackers | ARM (small cores) | milliwatts | read buttons and sensors |
| mobile | smartphones, tablets, handhelds | ARM | a few watts, battery | the largest gaming platform |
| personal | laptops, desktop PCs | x86-64 (some ARM) | 50–500 W | high-end and competitive games, development |
| console | PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch | x86-64 / ARM | 15–200 W | fixed hardware tuned for games |
| server | data centres, cloud | x86-64, ARM | kilowatts per rack | online play, accounts, cloud gaming |

: Classes of computing systems used in the games industry. {#tbl-classes}

Two observations follow. First, the classes differ less in *what* they can
compute than in *how much* and *at what energy cost*: a phone must deliver its
performance from a battery and without a fan, so mobile games must be designed
for strict limits of power and heat. Second, the performance of all classes
has grown exponentially for decades. In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the
number of transistors on a chip doubled at a regular interval, later stated as
about every two years. This trend, known as **Moore's law**, explains why a
phone today outperforms the game consoles of fifteen years ago, although the
growth has slowed as transistors approach physical limits.

## 1.4 Digital platforms in the games industry

To a player, "the platform" is the device in their hands. To the games
industry, a platform is more than hardware.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.3 — Digital platform"}
A **digital platform** is the combination of a hardware family, an operating
system, a set of programming interfaces and development tools (an *SDK*), and
a distribution channel with its own rules, on which software is built, sold
and run.
:::

![The four layers of a digital platform.](images/platform-stack.png){#fig-stack width=62%}

| Platform | Hardware | Operating system | Store |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android | phones and tablets of many manufacturers | Android | Google Play (and others) |
| iOS / iPadOS | iPhone, iPad | iOS, iPadOS | App Store |
| PC | Windows computers of many manufacturers | Windows | Steam, Epic Games Store, … |
| Consoles | PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch | system software of the console maker | the console maker's store |
| Cloud gaming | servers in data centres; any screen | runs on the server | subscription services |

: Major game platforms. {#tbl-platforms}

The owner of a platform controls access to its players. It decides which
programming interfaces games may use, which content is allowed, how payments
work and what share of each sale it keeps; it may require every game to pass a
certification process before release. Mobile is today the largest segment of
the games market, earning roughly half of global game revenue, which is why
this diploma concentrates on Android and iOS.

Because every platform is different, studios rarely write a separate game for
each. They use a **cross-platform** game engine, which hides the differences
behind one set of tools and generates a separate build per platform. The
differences do not disappear, however. Even within one platform the developer
faces **fragmentation**: Android alone runs on thousands of device models with
different processors, screen sizes and system versions. The consequences for
testing and publishing occupy weeks 10, 14 and 15 of this course.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.4 — Porting a mobile game to a console"}
A studio has released a puzzle game on Android and iOS and decides to bring it
to the Nintendo Switch. Using the levels and the platform definition, list what
changes.

1. **ISA**: the Switch also uses ARM, so the engine can generate native code
   for it; for an x86-64 console a different build would be needed.
2. **Input**: touch is available only in handheld mode; the game must also
   work with buttons and analog sticks.
3. **Output**: the TV screen is larger and landscape; the interface designed
   for a portrait phone must be re-laid out.
4. **Platform rules**: the studio needs a developer agreement and the console
   SDK, and the game must pass the console maker's certification before it can
   appear in the store.
:::

## Case study: Tap Runner

*Tap Runner* is a small endless-runner game: the character runs
automatically, and the player taps to jump over obstacles. The game is
released on Android, iOS and Windows PC and saves the best distance. The
mini-game below is a version of Tap Runner that shows, for every tap, which
part of the computing system is at work.

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 1
("Introduction"): structured computer organization, languages, levels and
virtual machines, milestones in computer architecture, and the "computer zoo".

## Exercises

1. Name the four functions of a computing system and give an example of each
   in a racing game.
2. Explain the key idea of the stored-program model and why it matters for a
   device that runs many different games.
3. A laptop CPU core runs at 2.4 GHz. How many clock ticks are available per
   frame at 120 fps?
4. A phone has 6 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. A player installs ten large
   games. Which of the two fills up? Which one fills up when the player keeps
   five games open at once?
5. Distinguish translation from interpretation, and name the program that
   performs each.
6. Why can an Android game not be copied unchanged to a Windows PC, even if
   both computers are equally powerful? Use the term ISA.
7. Arrange in order from the lowest level to the highest: operating system
   machine, digital logic, problem-oriented language, ISA, microarchitecture,
   assembly language.
8. Give two reasons why a game for phones must be designed differently from a
   game for a desktop PC, even when the phone is fast.
9. Using the definition of a digital platform, explain why the App Store is
   part of the iOS platform.
10. *Tap Runner* (case study): for one jump, state which part of the
    stored-program model is involved at each of the four functions.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Input: steering on the touch screen; processing: computing the car's movement and collisions; output: the frame and the engine sound; storage: saving the best lap.
2. Instructions are stored in memory like data, so a new program is run by loading new contents into memory.
3. $2.4 \times 10^9 / 120 = 2 \times 10^7$: 20 million ticks.
4. Installing fills the storage (128 GB); keeping games open fills the RAM (6 GB).
5. Translation converts the whole program before it runs (compiler, assembler); interpretation executes it instruction by instruction (interpreter).
6. The phone uses the ARM ISA and the PC x86-64; machine code for one ISA does not run on the other, so the game must be rebuilt.
7. Digital logic, microarchitecture, ISA, operating system machine, assembly language, problem-oriented language.
8. A battery-powered phone has a strict power and heat limit (no fan); it uses touch input and a small screen; it runs on many different device models.
9. A platform includes its distribution channel and rules; on iOS the App Store is the channel through which games are sold and installed, under Apple's rules.
10. Input device (touch screen) → CPU executes the jump logic using RAM → output devices (GPU and display, speaker) → storage device saves the best distance.
:::
